tasks.short: Register attendance, enter marks, note behaviour and contacts, check records before report deadlines and fix errors.

steps.what: Teacher registers attendance at the start of each lesson
Teacher enters marks in the student records: copied from the paper mark book pupil by pupil today; after the change digital tests import their marks and paper tests are typed on a class grid
Teacher checks the class's marks before they are released: imported and typed marks match the tests and the right pupils
Teacher releases the checked marks to pupils and parents in the student information system
Teacher writes notes on behaviour, parent contacts and support in free text
Teacher hunts for missing marks and unexplained absences before report deadlines
Attendance officer follows up unexplained absences with parents
Teacher corrects record errors that pupils or parents report

tasks.design: Marks from digital tests flow into the student information system ({OTHER}) through the test tool's export and are released to pupils and parents only after the teacher checks them, and paper tests are entered on a class grid instead of pupil by pupil. Notes use set types (behaviour, parent contact, support) with short templates, and a completeness view lists missing marks and unexplained absences per class ahead of each report deadline.
tasks.previous_blocker: Marks moved by hand from tests and mark books, and gaps were found only at report time.
tasks.enabler_now: Pupil records systems hold marks, goals and parent contact, and test tools export marks.
tasks.still_hard: Paper tests still need entry; support notes can contain health data that needs care.
tasks.human_edge: Writing a note that is fair to the pupil and useful to the mentor.
tasks.altitude: Nothing changes in decision rights; records are complete earlier with less copying.

reach.task: Prepare report cards and transfer files
reach.learn: Whether the completeness view cuts last-minute chasing of teachers.

evidence.claim: A Dutch pupil records system keeps pupil records, learning-goal tracking and a parent app.
Schools process pupil data under the public task; support needs can be health data; new pupil-data systems need a DPIA.
Staff, parents and pupils have consent rights on tools that can monitor staff and on pupil-data rules.

assumptions: Boundary: from attendance and marks to corrected records; report cards are outside.
Input contract: test marks exported by the digital test tool set up by the ICT coordinator; note types agreed by the school; fallback is entry by hand.
Attendance officer and parent time is outside the teacher's savings.
Attendance registration does not change.

Coverage for s2: about half of tests are taken in the digital test tool and export their marks, which keep about 10 for checks; paper tests are typed on the class grid, which keeps about 80; so s2 keeps 45. Marks are released only after the teacher's check (s2b, s2c).
Notes on behaviour, contacts and support are first records: s3 keeps 90, saving only the layout and the note type.
unknowns: Whether the test tool exports to the student information system.
research_questions: Do marks reach the records sooner after tests when imported?

already_counted.description: Teacher checks imported marks against the test.
Teacher reviews the completeness list before deadlines.

incremental.description: Teacher fixes failed or mismatched imports.
ICT coordinator keeps the test-to-record link working.

approvals.approved_version: The marks for this test and class exactly as checked by the teacher in s2b, released once to the pupils' and parents' view in the student information system; any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: subjects that test mostly on paper keep entering marks by hand on the grid, so s2 keeps 80 (21.3); high: half of tests digital as assumed (30.2).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Plan a lesson series that mixes instruction, demonstration and investigation, prepare materials, teach and share with colleagues.

steps.what: Teacher plans the lesson series with instruction, demonstration and investigation time

loop.input: The goals for the series from the school's fixed goal list, lesson count and length, the class's prior topic and the teacher's notes on what worked last year.
loop.output: A lesson-by-lesson outline with instruction, demonstration and work-time blocks and an investigation question per lesson.
loop.check: Every lesson must name at least one goal code from the fixed list and every goal must appear somewhere; block times must add up to the lesson length; the teacher reads each lesson against what the goal means for this class and rewrites lessons that do not fit. No pupil data goes into the draft.
loop.stop: One draft and one redraft; then the teacher plans alone.
loop.why_not_simpler: Balancing activities and writing investigation questions is creative work; a template only gives the empty grid.

steps.what: Teacher prepares demonstration set-ups and trial runs
Teacher writes investigation worksheets from scratch
Teacher gives instruction and demonstrations to students in class
Teacher guides work time and answers pupils' questions
Teacher e-mails the plan and worksheets to section colleagues

tasks.design: A bounded step drafts the lesson series outline from the school's fixed goal list and the teacher's notes, with every lesson tied to a goal code, and the teacher edits it. Worksheets start from the section's shared template library in {DOCS}, and the series is shared there instead of by e-mail; demonstrations and teaching stay as they are.
tasks.previous_blocker: Plans and worksheets were written from scratch each year and lived in personal folders.
tasks.enabler_now: Language models draft lesson plans; randomised trials in English schools found planning time fell with no quality loss.
tasks.still_hard: Use of planning assistants tends to fall off; drafts must fit this class and the lab equipment at hand.
tasks.human_edge: Running a demonstration that makes pupils ask why, and steering their investigation.
tasks.altitude: Nothing changes in decision rights; planning starts from an outline tied to goals.

reach.learn: Whether shared series plans let them prepare earlier.

evidence.claim: Among 259 science teachers in English secondary schools, a chatbot plus a guide cut weekly planning from 81.5 to 56.2 minutes with no quality difference (randomised, independent evaluation).
Among 464 primary teachers, a lesson assistant cut weekly preparation from 3.3 to 2.5 hours, but covered 7% of lessons and use declined over ten weeks (randomised, independent evaluation).
A Dutch adaptive practice product drafts a class activity for a lesson goal.
AI that evaluates learning outcomes is high-risk; drafting lesson plans is not listed.

assumptions: Boundary: from planning the series to sharing it; assessment is outside.
Input contract: the school's goal list per year and subject kept by the section head; template library kept by the section; fallback is planning from scratch.
The drafting tool is approved by the school after a privacy check, and no pupil data is entered.
Demonstrations, instruction and guidance do not change.
s1 keeps 70 because the teacher still decides the order and content of the series; the draft saves writing out the outline.
unknowns: Whether the section shares materials today.
How much planning the method's own materials already cover.
research_questions: Does use of the drafting step hold up after the first term?

already_counted.description: Teacher reviews and edits the drafted outline against goals and class.

incremental.description: Teacher writes the series notes the draft needs.
Section head keeps the goal list and template library current.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: a teacher using a complete published method plans little and uses few templates, so s1 and s3 keep 90 (6.0); high: series planned with the draft and templates (13.0).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Find who needs what from results and observation, group pupils, rewrite materials at other levels, set extra practice and update the group plan.

steps.what: Teacher reviews test results and observations to see which pupils need what
Teacher groups pupils for extra instruction or extension
Teacher rewrites texts and instructional materials at other reading levels or languages

loop.input: The original text or worksheet, the target level or home language, and the key terms the teacher marks as fixed.
loop.output: The text at the target level with the same tasks, plus a glossary of key terms.
loop.check: Every marked key term and every task must appear unchanged in meaning; the readability score must fall in the target band; answers in the key must not change; the teacher reads every version before handing it out.
loop.stop: One rewrite and one retry per text; then the teacher adapts by hand.
loop.why_not_simpler: Rewriting at another level while keeping the meaning is language work; a readability formula only measures it.

steps.what: Teacher puts together extra practice sheets for pupils who need it
Teacher varies teaching methods for groups in class
Teacher updates the group plan in a spreadsheet

tasks.design: A view in the student information system ({OTHER}) shows results per learning goal per pupil, and a bounded step rewrites texts at other reading levels or languages with key terms and tasks kept, for the teacher to read before use. Extra practice comes from the adaptive practice tool by learning goal, never to set a pupil's level or marks, and the group plan is generated from the groups the teacher sets.
tasks.previous_blocker: Rewriting materials for several levels took evenings, so most pupils got the same text.
tasks.enabler_now: Dutch lesson editors rewrite text at another level and translate, and adaptive practice tools assign exercises by goal.
tasks.still_hard: Rewrites can lose meaning in subject terms; tools that set levels or marks would be high-risk.
tasks.human_edge: Knowing what interests a pupil and which way of explaining will land.

ambition.what: Newcomer pupils and weak readers who get subject texts at their level in every lesson, not only in support hours.

tasks.altitude: The teacher checks adapted versions instead of writing them; grouping stays theirs.

reach.task: Adapt materials for pupils with an individual plan
reach.learn: Whether level rewrites meet their stricter needs.

evidence.claim: A Dutch lesson editor rewrites text at another level, summarises and translates.
A Dutch adaptive practice product offers practice and drafts class activities for a lesson goal.
AI that sets pupils' education level or evaluates learning outcomes is high-risk from 2 December 2027.

assumptions: Boundary: from reviewing results to the updated group plan; formal support plans are outside.

Input contract: marks per learning goal from the student information system; key terms marked by the teacher; practice items from the school's adaptive practice licence; fallback is hand-adapted sheets.
No pupil names or data go into the rewriting step.
Grouping and differentiated teaching do not change.
Input contract for s1: marks per learning goal exist only for digital tests whose items the method publisher tagged to goals, about half of tests; paper tests give a total mark only, so s1 keeps 60%.

s3 keeps 55 because the teacher reads every adapted version against the source; s6 keeps 60 because deciding who gets what support stays and only typing the plan goes. The ICT coordinator's tool approval and privacy check are one-off setup, not ongoing work.
unknowns: Whether marks are recorded per learning goal.
Number of pupils who need adapted texts per class.
research_questions: Do weak readers complete more tasks with level-adapted texts?

already_counted.description: Teacher reads every adapted text before handing it out.

incremental.description: Teacher marks key terms and target levels for each rewrite.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: few level differences or subjects heavy in diagrams, so rewrites are rarely used (s3 at 85) and results by goal are thin (s1 at 80) (15.2); high: as designed with half of tests by goal (25.7).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Watch and correct behaviour, record incidents and sanctions, inform mentor and parents, and handle repeated cases with the year coordinator.

steps.what: Teacher watches behaviour in class and corridors and corrects students
Teacher types incidents and sanctions under school policies into the record
Teacher checks the incident notice before it goes: code, a note in words fit for parents, the right pupil and recipients
Teacher sends the checked incident notice to the mentor and parents: by e-mail today, one release from the record after the change
Teacher deals with late pupils and pupils sent out of class
Teacher discusses repeated behaviour with the mentor and parents
Year coordinator decides on detention or suspension

tasks.design: Incident codes in the student information system ({OTHER}) let the teacher record lateness, phone use or disruption with two taps and a short note. After saving the entry, the teacher checks the notice and releases it once: the mentor is notified and, for the codes the school has agreed, parents get the message through the parent app.
tasks.previous_blocker: Each incident meant a free-text entry and separate e-mails to mentor and parents.
tasks.enabler_now: Pupil records systems have incident codes and parent apps with notifications.
tasks.still_hard: Enforcing rules is a relationship with pupils; which codes reach parents is a school policy that parents and staff must agree.
tasks.human_edge: Correcting a pupil firmly without losing them, and knowing when it is more than misbehaviour.
tasks.altitude: Nothing changes in decision rights; less writing per incident.

reach.task: Follow up incidents for their pupils
reach.learn: Whether instant notices help them act before patterns grow.

evidence.claim: A Dutch pupil records system includes a parent app for messages.
Parents, pupils and staff have consent rights on pupil-data rules and on tools that can monitor staff.
Inferring pupils' emotions with AI is banned; this design uses no AI.

assumptions: Boundary: from correcting behaviour to the sanction decision; suspension procedures are outside.
Input contract: incident codes and which codes notify parents agreed in the school's pupil-data rules with the participation council; fallback is free text and e-mail.
Year coordinator, mentor and parent time is outside the teacher's savings.
Correcting behaviour and conversations do not change.
s2 is part of keeping student records, which sibling task 25-2022.00:6579 covers; its saving is counted there, so s2 keeps its full time here.
s3 keeps 15 for the release; the check before it (s3b) keeps its full time.
unknowns: Number of incidents a teacher records per week.
Which codes parents want to hear about.
research_questions: Do instant notices change how quickly repeated behaviour is discussed?

incremental.description: School administrator keeps codes and notification rules current.
No new ongoing focal work; learning the codes is one-off.

approvals.approved_version: The incident notice with code and the teacher's note exactly as checked by the teacher in s3b, sent once to the pupil's mentor and, for codes the school agreed, to the parents through the parent app; any change needs a new check and a correction.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: many incidents need a personal e-mail or call beyond the coded notice, so s3 keeps 60 (3.7); high: most notices go as coded messages (8.0).

role.altitude: The middle school teacher keeps teaching, judgement and relationships; copying marks, rewriting texts and incident e-mails shrink.
role.ambitious_version: A teacher who gives every pupil a text they can read and spends evenings on lessons, not on admin.
